As for your question, humans have been aware of the existence of outer space for thousands of years. The earliest recorded observations of the night sky date back to ancient civilizations in Mesopotamia, Egypt, and Greece. These cultures recognized the stars and constellations, and some even believed in the existence of a spherical Earth.

The idea that space was a void of darkness illuminated only by stars and galaxies developed over time through the work of ancient Greek philosophers such as Aristotle and Eratosthenes. Eratosthenes, in particular, is credited with being the first person to accurately measure the circumference of the Earth and propose that it was a sphere.

The concept of a blue sky outside of Earth's atmosphere was not widely accepted until the 17th century, when scientists such as Galileo Galilei and Johannes Kepler began to study the behavior of light and the nature of the atmosphere. Galileo's observations of the sky using his telescope led him to conclude that the sky was not blue, but rather a result of the scattering of sunlight by the atmosphere.

It wasn't until the 19th century that the concept of a blue sky outside of Earth's atmosphere became more widely accepted, thanks in part to the work of scientists such as Joseph von Fraunhofer and Gustav Kirchhoff. Their research on the properties of light and the atmosphere helped to establish the modern understanding of the nature of space and the sky.
